analysis.one_liner: Sets a 30% minimum effective tax rate on annual incomes above $1 million.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 72 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone with adjusted gross income above $1 million a year to pay a minimum 30% tax on income above that threshold, after subtracting charitable donations. People already paying more than 30% between income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes would owe nothing extra, and the tax would phase in gradually. The money raised would go toward reducing the federal deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the general public would benefit through billions of dollars a year in deficit reduction, with the entire cost falling on households earning more than $1 million a year. The bill also stated that Congress should pursue broader tax reform closing loopholes and simplifying the system for ordinary filers.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a minimum 30% effective rate on adjusted gross income above $1 million (half that threshold for married filers filing separately), so very high earners can no longer pay a lower effective rate than middle-income families.
Counts income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes already paid toward the 30% floor, so the tax only applies to households whose total effective rate is currently below 30%.
Excludes charitable contributions from the taxed amount, so taxpayers could keep giving to charity without triggering a higher bill.
Raises revenue dedicated to reducing the deficit, and phases in gradually before fully applying to tax years after 2012, with the $1 million threshold adjusted for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Households with annual adjusted gross income above $1 million — roughly the top fraction of one percent of filers — would pay more, especially those whose income is largely capital gains or other income taxed at low rates. Some owners of large businesses that file as individuals would also be affected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

drawbacks.text: The bill adds yet another parallel tax calculation on top of the income tax and the alternative minimum tax, increasing complexity rather than simplifying the code; its own text acknowledges real reform should come later.
The revenue goes entirely to deficit reduction rather than to any direct benefit to households, so the gain to ordinary people is diffuse and invisible in daily life.
Taxpayers who do not itemize get no charitable exclusion under the bill's formula, so a non-itemizing donor with income just over the threshold could face a higher bill despite giving to charity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy is a targeted, well-guarded version of a minimum tax on millionaires: it protects charitable giving, counts taxes already paid, and phases in. The real costs are added tax complexity and higher bills for a very small group of high earners; the benefit to the public — deficit reduction — is real but diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Tammy Baldwin introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act of 2012 on February 6, 2012, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means that same day.
The bill would impose a 30% minimum tax rate on adjusted gross income above $1 million, excluding charitable contributions, with a phase-in and an inflation adjustment to the threshold.
72 members, all Democrats, signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill.
The Ways and Means Committee held no further action on the bill, and the complete action history ends with the sponsor's introductory remarks on February 7, 2012.
The bill also included a nonbinding statement that Congress should enact tax reform repealing loopholes, simplifying the system, and making the wealthiest taxpayers pay a fair share.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, the very highest earners kept paying effective rates that could fall below 30%, and no new revenue was raised to reduce the deficit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above $1 million kept their rates

for.name: Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor the day after introduction.

for.name: 72 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it substantial Democratic support but no Republican cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to itself and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought a minimum tax on millionaires to the House floor during the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 72 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican sponsorship, and the Republican-controlled committee and House never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have raised these households' effective tax rate to at least 30% on income above the threshold, with the revenue going to deficit reduction. Because the bill died, the group kept the existing rates, including low rates on capital gains income.

industries.industry: Private fund managers and investors living on capital gains
industries.note: Income taxed at preferential capital gains rates would have been pulled up toward the 30% minimum for million-dollar earners, the group that benefits most from the current rate gap. The bill's failure left that rate gap intact.

The bill carved charitable contributions out of the taxed amount, protecting large donors from a penalty for giving. Only donors who take the standard deduction rather than itemizing would have lost that protection.
